To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Parents and teenagers: please read the warning about fake pills

Please don’t scroll past this. The police warning about fake tablets is on here, but it needs more people to see it. I’m an ICU nurse and a mum. This is general safety advice, not a comment on Saturday or on anybody’s care. I’m not going to repeat rumours.

Police are warning about blue tablets being sold as diazepam or “Xanax” in south Manchester. Some have been found to contain nitazenes, synthetic opioids that can be far stronger than heroin. You cannot tell what’s in a tablet by looking at it, or trust that it contains what someone says it does.

The bit I really want parents and teenagers to hear is this: if someone goes down after taking something, ring 999 straight away. Don’t put them to bed to sleep it off. Don’t wait for them to come round. Don’t leave them alone.

Warning signs include being extremely drowsy or difficult to wake, tiny “pinpoint” pupils, slow or noisy breathing, and blue lips. You do not need to see every sign before calling. Noisy breathing in someone you can’t wake is not something to dismiss as snoring.

Tell the 999 operator where you are, what’s happening and anything you know about what they’ve taken. Put your phone on speaker and follow their instructions. If they’re unconscious but breathing normally, put them in the recovery position. If they aren’t breathing normally, tell the operator straight away and start CPR as instructed.

People can panic and think getting their mate into bed is looking after them. It isn’t safe. When breathing slows or stops, the brain isn’t getting enough oxygen. Waiting hours can mean irreversible brain injury or death. You don’t need to be certain what they’ve taken to get help.

And please, don’t delay because you’re frightened of getting into trouble. The police warning says it plainly: “Our priority is preserving life.” I can’t promise what happens afterwards, but fear of parents, school or police must not come before getting an ambulance.

There’s something practical you can do now, too. Naloxone nasal spray can reverse an opioid overdose, including one caused by nitazenes. It won’t reverse every drug’s effects, and it does not replace calling 999. If you have it, use it following the instructions. Further doses may be needed, and someone can become unwell again after it wears off. Stay with them until help arrives.

My notes for anyone wanting a kit: Brightpath drug & alcohol service on Stockport Road, next to the launderette, provides free nasal naloxone. Anyone can ask, no names needed. Training takes about 10 minutes. They’re open Monday to Friday, 10–4, and Thursday until 7.

I had this conversation with my lad, who’s 14, over his tea last night. There were eye rolls. But he listened, and he asked what pinpoint pupils meant. That’s a conversation worth having, even if they act like you’re doing their head in.

Parents and carers, please talk to your kids THIS week. Not after half term or when it feels easier. Tell them that if a mate is in trouble, they call 999 first. They don’t need your permission.

And please stop slagging kids off. Shame and judgement don’t make anyone safer. Scared kids hide things and hesitate to ring for help. We need them to know that getting help is the right thing to do.

Please share this, not just like it. Share the police warning as well. It needs to reach the teenagers who might be there when someone needs help, not just the adults already reading it.
